stops.title: Ottomans, Safavids and Mughals
stops.blurb: In 1453 the Ottoman sultan Mehmed II captured Constantinople and made it his capital; over time it came to be called Istanbul. In 1501 Ismail was crowned the first Safavid shah of Iran, and his successor Abbas moved the capital to Isfahan in 1597–98. In India, Babur defeated the Lodi sultan by 1527, and his grandson Akbar built the Mughal Empire.

stops.title: By sea around Africa to India

place.name: Cape of Good Hope, South Africa

stops.blurb: Portuguese crews had been sailing south along the West African coast since the mid-1400s. In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, the southern end of the continent. In 1497 Vasco da Gama followed, called at Mombasa and Malindi, where he hired an experienced navigator, and in May 1498 reached Calicut in India, a great port of the spice trade.

stops.title: Across the Atlantic and around the world
stops.blurb: In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for the Spanish crown, reached Guanahani in the Bahamas, home of the Taíno, the most numerous people of the Caribbean. He believed to the end that he had reached Asia. In 1519 five ships and 237 men left Seville under Ferdinand Magellan. One ship and 18 men came back in 1522, the first crew to sail around the world.
stops.dateNote: Magellan himself was killed in 1521 at Mactan in the Philippines, fighting forces led by Lapulapu; Juan Sebastián de Elcano brought the last ship home.

stops.title: The Columbian Exchange
stops.blurb: After 1492, crops, germs, ideas and people crossed the oceans between the Americas and the rest of the world. Maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes and cassava became staple foods in Africa, Asia and Europe, and chili peppers changed cooking from Hungary to Thailand. Wheat, sugar cane, coffee and bananas went the other way. So did smallpox, measles and other diseases new to the Americas.
stops.debate: How much the new crops raised Old World populations is still being measured. Nunn and Qian estimate the potato alone explains about an eighth of the population increase where it could be grown.

stops.title: The Great Dying in the Americas
stops.blurb: Smallpox, measles, typhus and other diseases from Afro-Eurasia reached peoples in the Americas who had never met them. Epidemics came in waves, alongside conquest and war. A 2019 review estimates that about 90 percent of the Indigenous population died within a century of 1492, some 56 million people. Central Mexico, home to just under 15 million people in 1519, had about 1.5 million a century later.
stops.debate: Published estimates of the population in 1492 range from about 8 million to over 110 million. Koch and colleagues combine them into a middle estimate of about 60 million.

links.label: Population history of the Indigenous peoples of the Americas

p: For thousands of years after the ice age, the peoples of the Americas and those of Africa, Asia and Europe grew different crops and lived with different diseases. Ocean voyages after 1492 ended that separation within a few generations. Historians call the result the Columbian Exchange: the transfer of crops, diseases, ideas, technologies and people between the two halves of the world.

From the Americas came four staple crops: maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes and cassava (also called manioc). They gave more calories, or grew in places where older staples did poorly. Tomatoes, chili peppers, cacao, peanuts and pineapples added little in calories but changed cooking across the world, from paprika in Hungary to curries in India and chili in Korea and Thailand. Tobacco went the same way. In the other direction went wheat, rice, sugar cane, coffee, soybeans, oranges and bananas. Diseases travelled too, with terrible effect in the Americas.

Much of the evidence is the world's diet today. Nathan Nunn and Nancy Qian point out that the top consumers of potatoes and of cassava are now all countries outside the Americas, and that maize supplies a large share of daily calories in many of them. Written records track when crops arrived: Flynn and Giráldez note that American crops reached Chinese farms through the Manila galleons, the Spanish ships that crossed the Pacific each year from 1565.

To measure effects, economists compare places that could grow a new crop with places that could not, before and after it arrived. Using this method, Nunn and Qian estimate that the potato explains about 12 percent of the rise in population, and nearly half the rise in the share of people living in cities, in the Old World countries suited to it.

The size of the crop effects depends on the method and the period chosen, so figures like these are estimates, not settled facts. The origin of venereal syphilis, which spread across Europe in the 1490s, was argued over for centuries. Nunn and Qian review genetic work by Harper and colleagues that places the bacterium's closest relatives in South America, which supports an American origin, though accounts of similar symptoms and skeletons with similar-looking scars from before 1492 kept the question open for a long time.

Few people today eat a meal that the Columbian Exchange did not shape. New crops helped feed growing populations in China, Africa and Europe. At the same time, the exchange carried the diseases that emptied much of the Americas, and the plantation crops whose demand for labour drove the transatlantic slave trade. The same voyages that enriched diets on one side of the world brought catastrophe to the other.

The peoples of the Americas had been separated from Africa, Asia and Europe since the end of the ice age. They had never been exposed to smallpox, measles, whooping cough, chicken pox, typhus or malaria. When these diseases arrived after 1492, they spread through populations with no immunity. Outbreaks came again and again over the following century and more, alongside conquest and war. During the siege of Tenochtitlan in 1521, defenders died of disease and hunger as well as in battle.

The Taíno of Hispaniola, among the first peoples to meet Columbus's crews, had almost disappeared within fifty years. Central Mexico, with just under 15 million people in 1519, had about 1.5 million a century later. The historian Noble David Cook estimated that the least affected regions lost 80 percent of their people, the worst affected lost everyone, and a typical society lost 90 percent.
Written records begin only after contact. Disease often travelled ahead of the Europeans who wrote things down, so the earliest losses went unrecorded and first-hand counts may be too low.

Ancient DNA now helps identify the killers. In 2018, Åshild Vågene and colleagues studied a cemetery at Teposcolula-Yucundaa in Oaxaca, linked to an epidemic of 1545 to 1550 that people in Mexico called *cocoliztli*. They recovered genomes of *Salmonella enterica* Paratyphi C, a cause of enteric fever, from ten of the dead, making it a strong candidate for that outbreak.

The scale also shows up in the natural world. In 2019, Alexander Koch and colleagues combined 119 published population estimates with evidence of land use. They estimate about 60.5 million people lived in the Americas in 1492 and that about 90 percent died within a century, roughly 56 million people. As fields were abandoned, forest and grassland grew back on about 56 million hectares and took up carbon from the air.

How many people lived in the Americas in 1492 is one of the longest arguments in the field. Estimates have ranged from about 8 million (Kroeber, 1939) to over 110 million (Dobyns, 1966), and Nunn and Qian note that decades of research have not narrowed the range. Koch and colleagues give a likely range of about 45 to 78 million. Because early observers may have seen populations already thinned by disease, both high and low estimates have kept their defenders.

Nunn and Qian describe the devastation as far greater than that of the Black Death in Europe. The loss of so many workers, together with demand for plantation crops, helped drive the transatlantic slave trade. Koch and colleagues argue that the regrowth of forests on abandoned land helps explain half or more of a drop in carbon dioxide in the late 1500s and early 1600s, a sign that human history and the Earth's climate were already tied together.
